PRORATION OF ESTATE TAXES AMONG BENEFICIARIES — WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet states what California law says about a question that arises only after the amount of the federal or California estate tax is already known: which recipients of Margaret C. Alvarado's property actually bear that tax, and in what shares. Material on estate tax generally answers a different question — how large the taxable estate is, what the exclusion amount is, what the marital deduction and portability do. Those rules fix the size of the bill. The rules described here fix its incidence.

The distinction matters most where property passes outside probate. A payable-on-death account, a transfer-on-death deed, a transfer-on-death security registration, life insurance, a joint tenancy and a funded revocable trust all move property to a recipient without administration, but property that moves that way is still in the federal gross estate if the Internal Revenue Code puts it there. California's answer is Probate Code Division 10 (§§ 20100–20225), which by default spreads the estate tax across everyone who receives property included in the gross estate — including the trustee of the Alvarado Family Trust — rather than leaving it on the probate estate alone, and which gives Dana Okonkwo both a right and a duty to collect from recipients whose property never reached the estate.

What follows sets out the statutory text of Chapter 1 (estate taxes) and the parallel Chapter 2 (generation-skipping transfer taxes), and the holdings of the published California opinions that construe them: Estate of Armstrong (1961) 56 Cal.2d 796, Estate of Malpas (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1901, Estate of Wathen (1997) 56 Cal.App.4th 48 and Estate of Hughes (2005) 133 Cal.App.4th 121. It is a description of statutes and published opinions prepared by Jordan Lee on September 15, 2026. It does not compute anyone's share, does not read Margaret C. Alvarado's will or trust, and does not tell Dana Okonkwo, any beneficiary or any non-probate recipient what to do.

THE DEFAULT RULE: ESTATE TAX IS EQUITABLY PRORATED AMONG ALL PERSONS INTERESTED IN THE ESTATE
Probate Code § 20110(a) states the default. Unless one of the two exceptions in subdivision (b) applies, any estate tax is to be equitably prorated among the persons interested in the estate in the manner prescribed by Article 2 of Chapter 1 (§§ 20110–20117). The chapter reaches both federal and California estate tax: § 20100(a) defines 'estate tax' as a tax imposed by any federal or California estate tax law, now existing or hereafter enacted, and includes interest and penalties on any deficiency. Proration is therefore the starting position in every California estate governed by the chapter, and a will or trust that says nothing about taxes leaves it in place.

The California Supreme Court described the policy behind the predecessor statute (former Probate Code §§ 970–977, adopted in 1943) in Estate of Armstrong, where the decedent's probate estate was appraised at $40,498 while her nieces took $198,215 under a revocable inter vivos trust whose assets were taxable at her death, and the death taxes on the whole taxable estate exceeded the value of the probate estate. The court said that, subject only to the expressed will of the testator to the contrary, proration of such taxes is part of the fundamental public policy of the state.

Chapter 1 has a date limit of its own: § 20101(a) provides that it does not apply to persons interested in the estate of a decedent who died before January 1, 1987, and § 20101(b) keeps the repealed former article applicable to those earlier deaths while directing that no inference about pre-1987 law be drawn from the enactment of the chapter.

WHO COUNTS AS A PERSON INTERESTED IN THE ESTATE, AND WHAT COUNTS AS PROPERTY
The reach of the proration chapter is set by two definitions in Probate Code § 20100. Under § 20100(b), a 'person interested in the estate' is any person, including a personal representative, entitled to receive, or who has received, from a decedent while alive or by reason of the death of the decedent any property or interest therein. Nothing in that definition requires the property to pass under a will or through administration. Under § 20100(d), 'property' means property included in the gross estate for federal estate tax purposes, and under § 20100(e), 'value' means fair market value as determined for federal estate tax purposes.

Read together, those definitions tie the class of people who bear the tax to the federal gross estate rather than to the probate estate. A recipient of a payable-on-death account, a transfer-on-death deed, a survivorship interest, a life insurance benefit or a distribution from a revocable trust is a person interested in the estate for purposes of this chapter to the extent what that person received is included in the federal gross estate, and the value used is the federal estate tax value, not any separate state appraisal. Estate of Armstrong illustrates the point under the predecessor statute, where the taxable estate consisted overwhelmingly of assets held in a revocable inter vivos trust that never entered probate.

THE PRORATION FORMULA: VALUE RECEIVED OVER TOTAL VALUE RECEIVED
Probate Code § 20111 supplies the arithmetic that § 20110(a) refers to. The proration is made in the proportion that the value of the property received by each person interested in the estate bears to the total value of all property received by all persons interested in the estate, subject to the rest of Article 2. Because § 20100(d) defines the relevant property as property in the federal gross estate and § 20100(e) defines value as federal estate tax value, the denominator of that fraction is the whole taxable estate and not the probate estate.

In Estate of Hughes the Court of Appeal described § 20110 and § 20111 as the governing statutes and treated the probate court's allocation according to the § 20111 formula as unobjectionable; what the court reversed was a separate charge the probate court had added on top of that allocation, discussed in a later clause of this sheet.

THE TAX CLAUSE EXCEPTION: A WRITTEN INSTRUMENT THAT SPECIFICALLY DIRECTS A DIFFERENT ALLOCATION
Probate Code § 20110(b)(1) is the first of the two exceptions to statutory proration. Proration does not apply to the extent the decedent, in a written inter vivos or testamentary instrument disposing of property, specifically directs that the property be applied to the satisfaction of an estate tax or that an estate tax be prorated to the property in the manner provided in the instrument. The same paragraph defines an 'instrument disposing of property' to include an instrument that creates an interest in property, and an amendment to an instrument that disposes of property or creates an interest in property.

Estate of Wathen applied that paragraph to a will and a living trust executed the same day as one integrated plan. The will directed that all death taxes attributable to the probate estate or to property passing outside it be charged to and paid out of the trust. The Court of Appeal held that a direction of that kind, construed with the aid of extrinsic evidence, satisfies § 20110(b)(1) and qualifies as a specific direction that the taxes be satisfied as directed rather than prorated under § 20110(a). The court also rejected the argument that the will could be ignored because it poured everything into the trust, reasoning that the will disposed of the entire estate and so was a testamentary instrument disposing of property within the meaning of the section.

Estate of Malpas records what changed in 1987. Under former § 970 the exception applied where a testator 'otherwise directs in his or her will'; the rewritten section narrowed it to a decedent who 'specifically directs' a method of payment or proration, which the Sixth District described as a restatement of the law including its judicial gloss.

HOW AN UNCLEAR TAX CLAUSE IS CONSTRUED: AMBIGUITIES ARE RESOLVED IN FAVOR OF APPORTIONMENT
Estate of Armstrong states the rule of construction that governs a tax clause which does not clearly displace proration. Surveying California and out-of-state authority under the predecessor statute, the Supreme Court said that apportionment is the general rule, that an exception is made only where there is a clear and unambiguous direction to the contrary, and that ambiguities are resolved in favor of apportionment. On the facts, a direction to the executor to pay 'all estate and inheritance taxes which may become due by my death, without limitation to property passing under my will' was held, at most, ambiguous, and so was not an express direction against proration.

Estate of Wathen addresses what evidence may be used on that question. Where an instrument contains a provision addressing proration but the provision is insufficiently clear to override § 20110, extrinsic evidence is admissible to construe the decedent's intent. The court drew the line at silence: it is only where the testamentary document fails altogether to refer to the allocation of taxes that extrinsic evidence is inadmissible, on the theory that silence cannot create an ambiguity. Wathen also held that where a will and a trust were executed as one integrated plan, both documents must be considered together and a direction contained in one but not the other is sufficient.

THE SECOND EXCEPTION: WHERE FEDERAL LAW DIRECTS THE MANNER OF PRORATION
The other exception, Probate Code § 20110(b)(2), gives way to federal law: the section does not apply where federal law directs otherwise, and if federal law directs the manner of proration of the federal estate tax, the California estate tax is prorated in the same manner. On its face the paragraph is a conflicts rule. It does not itself create any right to recover tax from anyone; the California recovery and reimbursement provisions are §§ 20116 and 20117, described in later clauses of this sheet.

Federal recovery statutes exist alongside it. Hoffman v. Connell (1999) 73 Cal.App.4th 1194, a dispute over California's former pick-up estate tax, quotes 26 U.S.C. § 2207A(a)(1), under which a decedent's estate is entitled to recover from the person receiving qualified terminable interest property the amount by which the total tax paid exceeds the tax that would have been payable had the property not been included in the gross estate. The court reasoned that the availability of statutory reimbursement from the trustees tended to show the estate was shouldering a tax burden based on assets the decedent did not own.

LIFE ESTATES AND OTHER TEMPORARY INTERESTS: THE TAX COMES OUT OF THE CORPUS
Probate Code § 20113 removes successive interests in one asset from the ordinary ratio. Where a trust is created, or other provision made, giving a person an interest in the income of, an estate for years or for life in, or another temporary interest in any property, the estate tax on both the temporary interest and on the remainder is charged against and paid out of the corpus of the property, without apportionment between remainders and temporary estates.

Estate of Malpas is the published construction of that section. A will with no tax clause gave a 68-year-old friend a life estate in a house, with the remainder falling into a residuary trust for relatives. The Sixth District held that the estate tax allocable to the house had to be paid, or reimbursed to the estate, from the house itself, and that the probate court could not release the house from estate taxes altogether over the remainder holder's objection. The court explained that by adopting a single rule for successive interests in liquid and illiquid assets alike, the Legislature made a judgment that taking the tax from the asset, and letting the proration work itself out over time, is more equitable than relying on actuarial tables or exempting one of the successive interests. It acknowledged the practical consequence for an illiquid asset: if the parties and the probate court can find no alternative, the asset may have to be sold to pay the tax § 20113 requires. The court remanded for a new order and directed that, if a sale proved necessary, the balance of the proceeds be divided between the life tenant and the trust according to the values of their respective interests at the time of sale.

RECOVERING THE TAX FROM PROPERTY THAT NEVER REACHED THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE
Probate Code § 20116(a) addresses the situation the definitions in § 20100 create. Where all property does not come into the possession of the personal representative, the personal representative is entitled, and has the duty, to recover from the persons interested in the estate the proportionate amount of the estate tax with which they are chargeable under the chapter. The statute states that as an obligation, not merely a power.

Section 20116(b) allocates the loss if collection fails. Where the personal representative cannot collect from a person interested in the estate the amount apportioned to that person, the amount not recoverable is equitably prorated among the other persons interested in the estate who are subject to proration, so a shortfall attributable to one recipient is spread across the remaining recipients rather than absorbed by the probate estate alone.

Probate Code § 20125 supplies a cross-border route. A personal representative acting or resident in another state may bring an action in California to recover from a person interested in the estate who is resident here or owns property here the amount of the federal estate tax, or an estate tax or death duty payable to another state, apportioned to that person. The action is brought in the superior court of any county in which administration of the estate would be proper or, if none, in which any defendant resides, and § 20125(c) makes the apportionment by the court administering the estate in the other state prima facie correct.

REIMBURSEMENT BETWEEN RECIPIENTS WHEN ONE OF THEM DOES NOT PAY
Probate Code § 20117 gives a recipient who ends up paying more than the share prorated to that recipient a claim against the recipient who did not pay. Section 20117(c) allows the personal representative or the person holding the right to commence a proceeding to have a court determine it, applies the Article 3 judicial procedure to that proceeding with the changes necessary to fit it, and makes the resulting order an enforceable judgment.

THE JUDICIAL PRORATION PROCEEDING, AND WHY IT IS OPTIONAL
Article 3 of Chapter 1 (Probate Code §§ 20120–20125) supplies a court procedure. Under § 20120(a), the personal representative or any person interested in the estate may commence a proceeding to have a court determine the proration. Venue is the court in which the estate was administered or, where no administration proceedings have been commenced, the superior court of any county in which the estate could be administered; where administration is pending the proceeding is combined with it, and § 20120(c) provides that a proceeding commenced at any time before final distribution carries no additional filing fee. Section 20121 requires a petition stating the jurisdictional facts and the other facts the court needs.

Notice is split by § 20122 according to what the court will order against the person. At least 30 days before the hearing the petitioner must deliver notice of the hearing and a copy of the petition, under Probate Code § 1215, to the personal representative and to each person interested in the estate against whom prorated amounts may be charged out of property the personal representative holds; and must cause a summons and a copy of the petition to be served, in the form and manner prescribed by Code of Civil Procedure title 5 (commencing with § 410.10), on each person who may be directed to pay prorated amounts over. Section 20123(a) directs the court to order the personal representative to charge prorated amounts against persons whose property it holds, and to order all other persons summarily to pay their prorated amounts to the personal representative; § 20123(b) makes that order a judgment enforceable against those persons.

Estate of Hughes describes the status of the whole procedure. When the proration statutes were reenacted in 1986 the Legislature omitted the provision that had required a court order to accomplish the proration, and the Court of Appeal concluded that the Article 3 proceedings are optional.

The reach of the proration chapter is set by two definitions in Probate Code § 20100. Under § 20100(b), a 'person interested in the estate' is any person, including a personal representative, entitled to receive, or who has received, from a decedent while alive or by reason of the death of the decedent any property or interest therein. A recipient of a payable-on-death account, a transfer-on-death deed, a survivorship interest, a life insurance benefit or a distribution from a revocable trust is a person interested in the estate for purposes of this chapter to the extent what that person received is included in the federal gross estate, and the value used is the federal estate tax value, not any separate state appraisal. Estate of Armstrong illustrates the point under the predecessor statute, where the taxable estate consisted overwhelmingly of assets held in a revocable inter vivos trust that never entered probate.

Estate of Armstrong states the rule of construction that governs a tax clause which does not clearly displace proration. Surveying California and out-of-state authority under the predecessor statute, the Supreme Court said that apportionment is the general rule, that an exception is made only where there is a clear and unambiguous direction to the contrary, and that ambiguities are resolved in favor of apportionment. Estate of Wathen addresses what evidence may be used on that question. Where an instrument contains a provision addressing proration but the provision is insufficiently clear to override § 20110, extrinsic evidence is admissible to construe the decedent's intent. The court drew the line at silence: it is only where the testamentary document fails altogether to refer to the allocation of taxes that extrinsic evidence is inadmissible, on the theory that silence cannot create an ambiguity. Wathen also held that where a will and a trust were executed as one integrated plan, both documents must be considered together and a direction contained in one but not the other is sufficient.

Probate Code § 20113 removes successive interests in one asset from the ordinary ratio. Where a trust is created, or other provision made, giving a person an interest in the income of, an estate for years or for life in, or another temporary interest in any property, the estate tax on both the temporary interest and on the remainder is charged against and paid out of the corpus of the property, without apportionment between remainders and temporary estates.

Estate of Malpas is the published construction of that section. A will with no tax clause gave a 68-year-old friend a life estate in a house, with the remainder falling into a residuary trust for relatives. The Sixth District held that the estate tax allocable to the house had to be paid, or reimbursed to the estate, from the house itself, and that the probate court could not release the house from estate taxes altogether over the remainder holder's objection. The court explained that by adopting a single rule for successive interests in liquid and illiquid assets alike, the Legislature made a judgment that taking the tax from the asset, and letting the proration work itself out over time, is more equitable than relying on actuarial tables or exempting one of the successive interests. It acknowledged the practical consequence for an illiquid asset: if the parties and the probate court can find no alternative, the asset may have to be sold to pay the tax § 20113 requires. The court remanded for a new order and directed that, if a sale proved necessary, the balance of the proceeds be divided between the life tenant and the trust according to the values of their respective interests at the time of sale.

Probate Code § 20116(a) addresses the situation the definitions in § 20100 create. Where all property does not come into the possession of the personal representative, the personal representative is entitled, and has the duty, to recover from the persons interested in the estate the proportionate amount of the estate tax with which they are chargeable under the chapter. Probate Code § 20125 supplies a cross-border route. A personal representative acting or resident in another state may bring an action in California to recover from a person interested in the estate who is resident here or owns property here the amount of the federal estate tax, or an estate tax or death duty payable to another state, apportioned to that person. The action is brought in the superior court of any county in which administration of the estate would be proper or, if none, in which any defendant resides, and § 20125(c) makes the apportionment by the court administering the estate in the other state prima facie correct.

Article 3 of Chapter 1 (Probate Code §§ 20120–20125) supplies a court procedure. Under § 20120(a), the personal representative or any person interested in the estate may commence a proceeding to have a court determine the proration. Venue is the court in which the estate was administered or, where no administration proceedings have been commenced, the superior court of any county in which the estate could be administered; where administration is pending the proceeding is combined with it, and § 20120(c) provides that a proceeding commenced at any time before final distribution carries no additional filing fee. Section 20121 requires a petition stating the jurisdictional facts and the other facts the court needs.

Notice is split by § 20122 according to what the court will order against the person. At least 30 days before the hearing the petitioner must deliver notice of the hearing and a copy of the petition, under Probate Code § 1215, to the personal representative and to each person interested in the estate against whom prorated amounts may be charged out of property the personal representative holds; and must cause a summons and a copy of the petition to be served, in the form and manner prescribed by Code of Civil Procedure title 5 (commencing with § 410.10), on each person who may be directed to pay prorated amounts over. Section 20123(a) directs the court to order the personal representative to charge prorated amounts against persons whose property it holds, and to order all other persons summarily to pay their prorated amounts to the personal representative; § 20123(b) makes that order a judgment enforceable against those persons.

Estate of Hughes describes the status of the whole procedure. When the proration statutes were reenacted in 1986 the Legislature omitted the provision that had required a court order to accomplish the proration, and the Court of Appeal concluded that the Article 3 proceedings are optional.

Probate Code § 20124 keeps a proration order provisional as to amount. On petition by the personal representative or any person interested in the estate, the court is to modify an order made under Article 3 whenever it appears that the estate tax as actually determined differs from the amount on which the court based the order.

Estate of Hughes marks the outer edge of what may be brought into the proration at all. There the probate court had charged specific-bequest beneficiaries with a share of another beneficiary's estimated future income taxes arising from a tax-planning loan transaction. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding that the estate tax proration provisions do not contemplate the consideration of future income tax consequences and that the statutory procedure for estate tax proration does not include consideration of income tax consequences. It reasoned that Article 2 authorizes allowances for estate tax credits, exemptions, deductions, interest and penalties under § 20112, and addresses particular future estate tax events in §§ 20114, 20114.5, 20115 and 20124, but makes no comparable provision for income taxes payable by distributees. The court added that unless income tax consequences can be ascertained with reasonable certainty for purposes of equitable reallocation at the time of distribution, beneficiaries are responsible for paying their own future taxes, and that immediate, ascertainable consequences may instead be handled separately as an adjustment of the kind made in Estate of Bixby (1956) 140 Cal.App.2d 326.

Chapter 2 of Division 10 (Probate Code §§ 20200–20225) repeats the structure of Chapter 1 for a different tax. Under § 20210(a), except as provided in subdivision (b), any generation-skipping transfer tax is to be equitably prorated among the transferees in the manner prescribed by Article 2 of that chapter. Section 20210(b) carries the same two exceptions: a written instrument transferring property in which the transferor specifically directs otherwise, and a contrary direction in federal law. Section 20211 states the formula in the proportion that the value of the property received by each transferee bears to the total value received by all transferees.

The remaining sections track their Chapter 1 counterparts with the trustee in the place of the personal representative: § 20212 allows for credits, exemptions, deductions, interest and penalties; § 20213 charges the tax on a temporary interest and the other interests in the same property to the corpus without apportionment; § 20214 gives the trustee the entitlement and the duty to recover from transferees and reprorates what cannot be collected; § 20215 creates the right of reimbursement and subrogation; and Article 3 (§§ 20220–20225) supplies the judicial procedure.
